uncited: This family of techniques incorporates geometric constraints into the radiance field optimization loop to improve reconstruction quality, particularly in low-data regimes or when explicit geometry is required for downstream tasks.
While standard NeRF optimization relies solely on photometric RGB losses, these methods introduce depth-related penalties or sampling strategies.

Depth Supervision explicitly minimizes the difference between rendered depth and ground-truth depth (derived from SfM keypoints or stereo), whereas Pseudo-Depth approximates surface geometry via weighted averaging of sampled points to guide feature distillation or segmentation without requiring explicit depth labels.
All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework.
The core mechanism involves computing a depth estimate $\hat{D}(r)$ for a ray $r$ during the forward pass of the renderer and incorporating this value into the loss function or sampling strategy.

Here, $\sigma_i$ is the volume density, $\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$ is the interval between adjacent samples, and $T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$ is the accumulated transmittance up to sample $i$.
This formulation ensures that depth contributions are proportional to the opacity of the surface encountered at that depth.
This variant applies explicit depth supervision to the TensoRF architecture to enhance performance in low-data scenarios.
It differs from standard NeRF depth supervision by leveraging TensoRF's tensor decomposition for efficiency, while using COLMAP keypoints to generate sparse ground-truth depth labels.
*   **Loss Choice:** MSE loss was implemented as a baseline.
This technique approximates surface geometry without explicit depth labels.
It is primarily used in feature field distillation (e.g., for CLIPNeRF) to enable efficient sampling around the "surface" for feature extraction.
This method is employed for computational efficiency in feature rendering, avoiding the complete process of volume rendering for features.
This method generates ground-truth depth for novel panoramic views by projecting 2D pixel coordinates onto a uniform sphere centered at the camera position.
It enables the extraction of depth priors for 360-degree scenes.
The network parameters $\theta$ are optimized using RGB-D frames.
Depth supervision in NeRF-like models originated from the observation that photometric loss alone often leads to ambiguous geometry, especially in textureless regions or with sparse inputs.
